Method.metaDescription: Guides, a grid, a typeface, one colour. The five-step process behind every project.

hero.subtitle: Five steps. Same order, every time. It's the reason the tenth change is faster than the first.

guides.title: Guides first
guides.body: Every project starts with two vertical lines and two horizontal ones. Before colour, before type, before code. The skeleton decides everything that follows.

grid.title: A grid to hold it
grid.body: Twelve columns, consistent gutters, one maximum width. The grid is what makes the page feel calm at every screen size — and what makes the tenth change faster than the first.

restraint.title: Restraint
restraint.body: One typeface. Three colours. An accent that appears rarely. The beauty of the site comes from what is left out, not from what is added.

ownership.title: Ownership
ownership.body: One person holds the method from start to finish. No handoffs, no communication errors, no lost intent. You talk to the person who designs and builds.

steps.title: Five steps, in this order, every time.

lines.title: Lines first
lines.body: Before anything is styled, I lay out the guides. Two vertical edges for the content, two horizontal rules for the top of the headline and the baseline of the navigation. Everything after this either fits inside them or moves for a deliberate reason.

grid.title: A grid to hold it
grid.body: Twelve columns, consistent gutters, a maximum content width. The grid is the reason the site feels calm at every screen size. It is a promise about where things sit, and every element that comes later keeps that promise or explains why not.

type.title: Type, chosen for the job
type.body: One typeface, maybe two. Sizes and line breaks tuned line by line. Weight contrast used only where it earns its place. Type is the tone of voice — it carries more of the design than any image ever will.

colour.title: One colour that earns its place
colour.body: Paper, ink, one accent. In Khalai's case, a terracotta borrowed from Kenyan sunsets. It appears rarely and means something each time it does. A palette is a suggestion. A commitment is a decision.

code.title: Hand-written code
code.body: What I draw, I build. No page builders, no plugin stacks. Readable code that compiles in five years and does not need an upgrade. The discipline of the layout carries through to the discipline of the components.

grid.title: A grid that holds the page together.
grid.body: Twelve columns. Consistent gutters. A single maximum width. Watch the sample blocks snap into place — that's not decoration, it's the reason nothing on this site ever feels slightly off.
grid.caption: Every block on the site sits on one of these twelve columns. When something doesn't, it's because the exception is the point.

type.title: One typeface. Every size it needs to be.
type.body: Six sizes, one family. Each one chosen for a specific job. The type scale below is the actual scale the site uses — nothing is made up for this demo.
type.caption: Six sizes. One typeface. That's the entire typographic system.

colour.title: Three colours. No more.
colour.body: Paper, ink, accent. The accent — a Kenyan terracotta — appears only when something deserves emphasis. The rest is deliberately quiet.
colour.caption: The three colours behind every page on this site.

code.title: The components write themselves.
code.body: By the time I open the code editor, everything is decided. The code below is the actual component behind the capabilities section on the landing page — no abstractions added for the demo.
code.caption: Every component on this site was written by hand, following the same five-step method.

cta.title: The method works. Let's apply it.
cta.body: A short conversation, an honest assessment, and a written quote at a fixed price. If the method doesn't fit your project, I'll tell you that too.

agents.title: Agent networks, digitised
agents.body: The M-Pesa agent is the original fintech. Digitising the agent relationship — balances, float, disputes — is still underbuilt.

voice.title: Voice-first checkouts
voice.body: For users who can't read a form but can speak. A voice checkout that captures name, amount, and PIN by speech is closer than it looks.

offline.title: Offline-first payments
offline.body: Low-connectivity payments that queue on the device and settle when the network returns. Rural areas and matatus still need this.

credit.title: Embedded credit
credit.body: Buy-now-pay-later built on M-Pesa history, not credit scores. The data exists. The flow doesn't yet.

hero.titleLens: M-Pesa isn't a payment option. It's |the| payment method.
hero.subtitle: Half of Kenya pays by phone. If your checkout treats M-Pesa as a fallback behind a card form, you've already lost. Here's how I build for the flow your users actually use.

why.title: Three reasons M-Pesa deserves first-class treatment.
why.subtitle: Not because it's trendy. Because it's what your users are already holding in their hands.

default.title: It is the default
default.body: Over 90% of Kenyan adults use M-Pesa. When it's the primary payment method, the phone number field becomes the most important input on the page — and everything else adjusts.

mobile.title: It lives on the phone
mobile.body: The user is holding the device that will complete the payment. Every step of the flow should assume that — the input mode, the copy, the confirmation, the receipt.

trust.title: Trust is earned in seconds
trust.body: A payment page that doesn't look native to Kenyan users reads as suspicious. A page that speaks M-Pesa's language reads as familiar. The difference is subtle and it decides conversions.

principles.title: Four principles I don't compromise on.

ask.title: Ask only for what you need
ask.body: The phone number. The amount. That's it. Every additional field on a payment page is friction you're choosing to introduce.

frame.title: Frame the action in M-Pesa's language
frame.body: "Enter your PIN" — not "complete transaction". "Check your phone for the M-Pesa prompt" — not "awaiting payment confirmation". Speak to what the user is doing.

confirm.title: Confirm unambiguously
confirm.body: State the amount, the recipient, and the next step. "KES 2,500 paid to Mavuno Ltd. A receipt is on its way to your email." Not "Success".

recover.title: Recover from failure with dignity
recover.body: Every error message names what happened and what to do next. "M-Pesa could not be reached. Try again in a moment." Not "Error 403".

anatomy.title: What a good M-Pesa checkout says at each step.

phone.label: Entering the phone
phone.value: Phone number field labelled "M-Pesa phone", with +254 pre-filled and tel keyboard on mobile.

amount.label: Showing the amount
amount.value: Button reads "Pay KES 2,500", not "Continue". Currency, amount, and verb are all explicit.

action.label: Prompting the PIN
action.value: "Check your phone for the M-Pesa prompt. Enter your PIN to confirm."

wait.label: While it processes
wait.value: "Confirming your payment — this takes about 10 seconds."

done.label: When it succeeds
done.value: "KES 2,500 paid to Mavuno Ltd. A receipt is on its way to your email."

fail.label: When it fails
fail.value: "M-Pesa could not be reached. Try again in a moment, or use a different payment method."

About.subtitle: Khalai is a one-person design and software studio in Nairobi. I build things that ship, and stay shipped.
About.locationLine: Nairobi, Kenya · Working with teams across East Africa and beyond
About.story: Handing work between a designer and a developer costs more than it saves. Every handoff loses intent — a corner radius becomes a rounding error, a spacing rhythm becomes an approximation. Khalai is one person doing both: design and code from the same mind, at the same moment. It is slower to say yes. It is faster to ship.
About.intro: I grew up in Nairobi. I learned to build software on a laptop with a bad battery and a mobile connection that dropped every ten minutes. That taught me to write things that work under real constraints — low bandwidth, small screens, occasional power. If it runs here, it runs anywhere.

faq.title: Frequently asked
faq.subtitle: The questions we get most often, answered honestly.

reach.a: Within one business day. If you use WhatsApp, usually within the hour during Nairobi business hours.

timezone.q: I'm in a different timezone. Can we still work together?
timezone.a: Yes. Most of our clients are outside Kenya. We schedule calls to overlap with your working hours and reply to emails across a wide window.

budget.q: I don't know my budget yet. Is that a problem?
budget.a: Not at all. Bring us the problem and the outcome you want. We will help you understand what it costs, and why, before you commit to anything.

payment.a: Typically 40% to start, 60% on delivery. For larger projects we split into milestones. We accept M-Pesa, bank transfer, and card payments.

remote.q: Do you work with clients outside Kenya?
remote.a: Yes — most of our work is remote. We have shipped projects for clients in Uganda, Rwanda, Tanzania, the UK, and Germany.
